'''Kilmarnock Football Club''' is a Scottish professional [[Association football|football]] team based in the town of [[Kilmarnock]] in [[East Ayrshire]], that currently plays in the {{Scottish football updater|Kilmarno}}. The club has achieved several honours since its formation in 1869,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kilmarnockfc.co.uk/|title=Official Website of Kilmarnock FC|website=Kilmarnockfc.co.uk|access-date=22 June 2011|archive-date=17 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210217184906/http://www.kilmarnockfc.co.uk/|url-status=live}}</ref> most recently the [[2011–12 Scottish League Cup]] after a [[2012 Scottish League Cup final|1–0 win]] over [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]] at [[Hampden Park]]<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/17330246|title=Celtic 0–1 Kilmarnock|publisher=BBC Sport|date=18 March 2012|access-date=12 February 2018|archive-date=6 January 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160106020401/http://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/0/football/17330246|url-status=live}}</ref> and the [[Scottish Championship]] title in 2022. The club nickname, ''Killie'', is the Scottish term for the town of Kilmarnock.

The club have qualified for European competitions on nine occasions, their best performance coming in the [[1966–67 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup|1966–67 Fairs Cup]] when they progressed to the semi-finals, eventually being eliminated by [[Leeds United F.C.|Leeds United]]. The club is also one of only a few Scottish clubs to have played in three European competitions ([[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]], [[UEFA Cup Winners' Cup|Cup Winners' Cup]] and the [[UEFA Europa League|UEFA Cup]]).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.killiefc.com/Web%20Pages/EuroKillie.htm|title=Killie in Europe!!|website=Killiefc.com|access-date=30 July 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131121044922/http://www.killiefc.com/Web%20Pages/EuroKillie.htm|archive-date=21 November 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> Additionally, the club have played in the [[International Soccer League]] four times – [[1960 International Soccer League|1960]], [[1961 International Soccer League|1961]], [[1963 International Soccer League|1963]] and [[1965 International Soccer League|1965]], as well as competing in the [[1995 Korea Cup]].<ref name="Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd">{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=140}}</ref> Their most recent appearance in European competition football was during the [[2024–25 UEFA Europa League]] and [[2024–25 UEFA Conference League]].<ref>{{cite web |title=The official website for European football |url=https://www.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/clubs/62178--kilmarnock/ |website=[[UEFA]] |access-date=30 August 2024 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The official website for European football |url=https://www.uefa.com/uefaconferenceleague/clubs/62178--kilmarnock/ |website=[[UEFA]] |access-date=30 August 2024 |language=en}}</ref>

Kilmarnock Football Club is currently the oldest football club in the [[Scottish Premiership]], and also the second-oldest professional club in Scotland.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.scotsman.com/news/who-are-scotland-s-oldest-professional-football-clubs-1-4098282|title=Who are Scotland's oldest professional football clubs|website=Scotsman.com|access-date=21 May 2017|archive-date=1 June 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170601094134/http://www.scotsman.com/news/who-are-scotland-s-oldest-professional-football-clubs-1-4098282|url-status=live}}</ref> Home matches are played at [[Rugby Park]], a 15,003 capacity [[all-seater stadium]] situated in the town itself. Kilmarnock took part in the first-ever official match in the [[Scottish Cup]] against the now-defunct [[Renton F.C.|Renton]] in 1873. With a long-standing football rivalry with fellow [[Ayrshire]] side [[Ayr United F.C.|Ayr United]], both teams play frequently in the [[Ayrshire derby]], first meeting in September 1910.

==History==
{{See also|List of Kilmarnock F.C. seasons}}

===Formation and early years===
[[File:KilmarnockFC League Performance.svg|thumb|A history of Kilmarnock FC's overall league position from 1895 to 2025]]
[[File:Kilmarnock Football Club, 1878-1879.jpg|thumb|right|Earliest known photograph of Kilmarnock Football Club, 1878–1879]] 
The club's foundation dates back to the very earliest days of organised football in Scotland, with speculation over the club's beginnings being in 1868, 1869 or 1872 often disputed.<ref name="Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years">{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=3}}</ref> The club was founded by a collection of men and boys who were sporting enthusiasts, with a few of them playing [[cricket]] during the summer months, as well as playing [[bowls]], [[quoits]], [[running]] and [[golf]].<ref name="Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years"/> During the winter period, the group lacked active sporting opportunities, and in the Autumn of 1868, the younger members of the sporting enthusiasts who attended [[Kilmarnock Academy]] first played football in the Barbadoes Green area of Kilmarnock.<ref name="Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years"/> Football in Scotland at this time was considered "rough" and "disorderly", and, while it was popular, it had never been played in an organised manner before.<ref name="Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years"/> The group of sporting enthusiasts later became known as the club's "founding fathers", and began playing football with their own set of rules which were more similar to that of [[Rugby league]], rather than association rules, which had become the rules used for a similar game, also known as football, in England in the late 1850s.<ref name="Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years"/> A committee was formed with the intention of the game becoming more organised, and after raising money, had placed an advertisement in the 2 January 1869 issue of the ''[[Kilmarnock Standard]]'' for a general meeting of the "Kilmarnock Foot-ball Club" to be held in Robertson's Temperance Hotel on Portland Road in Kilmarnock on Tuesday 5 January 1869.<ref name="Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years"/> The advert read: "Parties wishing to become members may do so at the meeting, or at the Secretary's, 55 King Street".<ref name="Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years"/> No official recorded minutes or outcomes of the meeting are known to have existed.<ref name="Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years"/>

With no recorded minutes of the meeting having taken place in January 1869, it is assumed that the members continued to play amongst themselves and with their own set of rugby-inspired rules.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=9}}</ref> On 25 October 1872, a meeting was held by the committee at the [[George Hotel, Kilmarnock]]. Recorded minutes from the meeting highlighted that interest in the game had increased as had the membership, leading to the decision being made to officially constitute the club as "Kilmarnock Football Club", with a set of rules to play the game of football properly to be purchased, as no other clubs were playing "football" in the same style that the club had been playing up until that point.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> A meeting held by the committee on 29 October 1872 saw the agreement between the club and a gentleman, Mr. Wright, to rent his field nearby for £3, which they did until March 1873.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> A game was agreed to be played on the field on 2 November 1872, but no result or opponent to Kilmarnock Football Club were ever recorded.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> In November 1872, the club decided to formally adopt the [[rugby union]] rules they had purchased for use in the game.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> On 7 December 1872, Kilmarnock Football Club played their first known competitive game using the rugby union rules. The game was an 11-a-side game against Kilmarnock Cricket Club Xl which ended in a 0–0 draw.<ref name="ReferenceA"/>

[[File:Kilmarnock Football Club, 1897.jpg|thumb|left|Kilmarnock win the [[Scottish Qualifying Cup]], 1897]]

During a club meeting on 3 March 1873, a letter from [[Queen's Park F.C.|Queen's Park]] asked Kilmarnock F.C. if they were interested in attending a meeting at the Dewar Hotel in [[Glasgow]] on 13 March 1873 to discuss the formation of a [[Scottish Football Association]] playing to [[football association]] rules, with the possibility of purchasing a cup for the winner of a knock out competition to take place later in 1873.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> Kilmarnock had long previously turned Queen's Park's requests down in the past, however, a favourable letter was returned to the team, informing the club that Kilmarnock were unable to send a representative to the meeting in Glasgow on 13 March 1873 due to having a committee meeting on the scheduled date, but advised that they were willing to join the Scottish Football Association, pledging to pay the 5 shillings membership fee and donate £1 towards the purchase of a cup for the knock-out competition.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> The first game played by Kilmarnock under football association rules was in the 1873–74 season.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=10}}</ref> The club suffered a drastic decline in membership numbers following a fall out with their landlord at Holm Quarry, after the club wished to move back to Dundonald Road.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=12}}</ref> Kilmarnock Football Club were one of the founding members of the Ayrshire Football Association which formed in May 1877.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=14}}</ref> By the 1880s, Kilmarnock Football Club had established themselves as the premier club in [[Ayrshire]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=16}}</ref>

The club had not been considered eligible for the [[Scottish Football League]] when it was formed in 1890, nor was it deemed eligible to be included in a second division.<ref name="ReferenceB">{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=18}}</ref> Kilmarnock Football Club was finally elected to the Scottish League in 1895, and finished their first season in the Scottish League in fourth place out of ten teams.<ref name="ReferenceB"/> In [[1919–20 Scottish Cup|1920]] Kilmarnock won the Scottish Cup for the first time, beating [[Albion Rovers F.C.|Albion Rovers]] at [[Hampden Park]].<ref>{{cite web|title=17-04-1920 Albion Rovers (N) Scottish Cup Final {{!}} Killie Win Their 1st of 3 Scottish Cups|url=http://www.killiefc.com/en/17-04-1920-albion-rovers-n-scottish-cup-final_49428/|website=KillieFC|access-date=23 August 2020|archive-date=18 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190818005453/https://www.killiefc.com/en/17-04-1920-albion-rovers-n-scottish-cup-final_49428/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=herald20>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=_sRAAAAAIBAJ&sjid=JKYMAAAAIBAJ&pg=4461%2C6175898 |title=Kilmarnock, 3; Albion Rovers, 2. Scottish Cup–Final Tie |newspaper=[[The Glasgow Herald]] |date=19 April 1920 |page=13 |access-date=23 August 2020 |archive-date=30 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201030102215/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=_sRAAAAAIBAJ&sjid=JKYMAAAAIBAJ&pg=4461,6175898 |url-status=live }}</ref> This was followed by their second success in [[1928–29 Scottish Cup|1929]] where they beat massive favourites [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] 2–0 at the national stadium in front of a crowd of 114,708 people.<ref name="Ross 1994">{{cite book {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201024135859/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=8UA_AAAAIBAJ&sjid=tkwMAAAAIBAJ&pg=5970,1100284 |date=24 October 2020 }}, ''[[The Glasgow Herald]]'', 8 April 1929</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=06-04-1929 Rangers (N) Scottish Cup Final {{!}} Killie Win The Cup for the Second Time|url=https://www.killiefc.com/en/06-04-1929-rangers-n-scottish-cup-final_49427/|website=KillieFC|access-date=23 August 2020|archive-date=10 August the same opposition in [[1931–32 Scottish Cup|1932]] but this time were beaten after a replay,<ref>[https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=f1VRAAAAIBAJ&sjid=JjQNAAAAIBAJ&pg=4341%2C7659715 Rangers Win receiving end of an upset.<ref name=herald38r>[https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=c0FAAAAAIBAJ&sjid=iVkMAAAAIBAJ&pg=5874%2C4490760 East Fife Win On Their Merits | Second League Side Last Pace ===North American and European tournaments===

After finishing as runners-up during the [[1959–60 Scottish Division One|1959–60 season]], Kilmarnock could have been put forward as one of Scotland's entrants for the following season's [[Inter-Cities Fairs Cup|European Fairs Cup]].<ref name="ReferenceC">{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=72}}</ref> Instead, the Scottish Football Association sent the team to [[North America]] to play in the [[International Soccer League]], serving as Scotland's representative.<ref name="ReferenceC"/> Kilmarnock remained unbeaten during their group matches in both [[New York (state)|New York]] and [[Jersey City]], with wins over [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]] and English league champions, [[Burnley F.C.|Burnley]].<ref name="ReferenceC"/> Kilmarnock returned to North America to play in the International Soccer League final, losing 2–0 to Brazilian club [[Bangu Atlético Clube]].<ref name="ReferenceC"/>

During the [[1960–61 Scottish Division One|1960–61 season]], Kilmarnock reached the [[Scottish League Cup]] final for the second time, where they lost to [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] 2–0 and finished as the season's runners-up.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=75}}</ref> After years of being sidelined by the Scottish Football Association, Kilmarnock were put forward for the 1964–65 European Inter-Cities Fairs Cup, losing their first match.<ref name="ReferenceD">{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=90}}</ref> The team made it to the second round, losing to [[Everton F.C.|Everton]] 1–4 and exiting the competition.<ref name="ReferenceD"/>

===Scottish League Champions===

Kilmarnock performed strong during the [[1964–65 Scottish Division One|1964–65 season]], winning their first six matches in the season and remaining unbeaten in the league until December 1964.<ref name="ReferenceE">{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=92}}</ref> In [[1964–65 Scottish Division One|1964–65]] [[Heart of Midlothian F.C.|Heart of Midlothian]] fought out a championship title race with [[Willie Waddell]]'s Kilmarnock. In the era of two points for a win Hearts were three points clear with two games remaining. Hearts drew with [[Dundee United F.C.|Dundee United]] meaning the last game of the season with the two title challengers playing each other at Tynecastle would be a league decider. Kilmarnock needed to win by a two-goal margin to take the title. Hearts entered the game as favourites with both a statistical and home advantage. 

They also had a solid pedigree of trophy-winning under Tommy Walker. Waddell's Kilmarnock in contrast had been nearly men. Four times in the previous five seasons they had finished league runners-up including Hearts' triumph in 1960. Killie had also lost three domestic cup finals during the same period including the 1962 League Cup Final defeat to Hearts. Hearts had won five of the six senior cup finals they played in under Walker. Even the final they had lost was in a replay after drawing the first game. Hearts' [[Roald Jensen]] hit the post after six minutes. Kilmarnock then scored twice through [[Davie Sneddon]] and Brian McIlroy after 27 and 29 minutes. [[Alan Gordon (Scottish footballer)|Alan Gordon]] had an excellent chance to clinch the title for Hearts in second half injury time but was denied by a [[Bobby Ferguson (footballer, born 1945)|Bobby Ferguson]] diving save pushing the ball past the post. The 2–0 defeat meant Hearts lost the title by an average of 0.042 goals.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://footballpink.net/2013/09/22/killies-final-day-victory-breaks-hearts/|title=Killie's final day victory breaks Hearts|date=30 October 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161030142924/https://footballpink.net/2013/09/22/killies-final-day-victory-breaks-hearts/|access-date=2 November 2021|archive-date=30 October 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/196504241.html|title=1965-04-24 Sat Hearts 0 Kilmarnock 2|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=24 May 2017|archive-date=10 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160310124641/http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/196504241.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-93_7Gz5FTQ| archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211107/-93_7Gz5FTQ| archive-date=2021-11-07 | url-status=live|title=Hearts 0 Killie 2 (24/04/1965)|date=10 July 2008|via=[[YouTube]]}}{{cbignore}}</ref> Subsequently, Hearts were instrumental in pushing through a change to use goal difference to separate teams level on points. Ironically this rule change later denied Hearts the title in 1985–86.<ref name = hist64-74>{{cite web|url=http://www.heartsfc.co.uk.p.preprod.performgroup.com/articles/20061108/1964-1974_2241543_1458271|title=Hearts History 1964 – 74 www.heartsfc.co.uk|access-date=24 May 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160521154848/http://www.heartsfc.co.uk.p.preprod.performgroup.com/articles/20061108/1964-1974_2241543_1458271|archive-date=21 May 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> This is the only time to date Killie have been Scottish champions.

===Korean Cup and Scottish Cup victory===
[[File:Kilmarnock F.C., Scottish Cup Winners 1997.jpg|thumb|left|Kilmarnock F.C. arrive back in the town following their [[1997 Scottish Cup final]] victory, 24 May 1997]] 

Decline in the 1980s brought relegation to the [[Scottish Football League Division Two|Second Division]], returning to the top division with promotion in [[1992–93 in Scottish football|1993]]. In the summer of 1995, Kilmarnock were invited to [[South Korea]] to play in the [[Korea Cup]].<ref name="Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd"/> Kilmarnock played the [[Costa Rica national football team]], finishing the game with a draw between both teams.<ref name="Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd"/>

By the commencement of the [[1996–97 in Scottish football|1996–97 season]], optimism within the club remained low, with little to suggest that the season would see Kilmarnock win the Scottish Cup again, having previously done so 68 years prior.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=143}}</ref> With inconsistent league results, and a home defeat to [[Raith Rovers F.C.|Raith Rovers]] in December 1996, [[Bobby Williamson]] became the new manager of Kilmarnock and began introducing new players to the team.<ref name="ReferenceF">{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=142}}</ref> Players such as [[David Bagan]] and [[Alex Burke]] were credited with improving the team's performance, along with Williamson's managerial style and approach.<ref name="ReferenceF"/> With relegation still a possibility, Kilmarnock climbed out of the relegation zone following a 1–1 home draw in the final league match of the season between [[Aberdeen F.C.|Aberdeen]].<ref name="ReferenceF"/> During the same period, Kilmarnock had been making good progress in the Scottish Cup, progressing to the [[1997 Scottish Cup final]] with [[Falkirk F.C.|Falkirk]] held at [[Ibrox Stadium]] in Glasgow on 24 May 1997.<ref name="ReferenceF"/> 25,000 Kilmarnock fans attended with final, with [[Paul Wright (footballer)|Paul Wright]] scoring for Kilmarnock, allowing for Kilmarnock to claim the Scottish Cup for the third time.<ref name="ReferenceF"/> Following their Scottish Cup victory, the team travelled back to Kilmarnock from Glasgow on an open topped bus, travelling up the town's John Finnie Street where they were met with a barrage of fans celebrating their victory.<ref name="ReferenceF"/>

Victory in the Scottish Cup secured a place for Kilmarnock in the [[1997–98 UEFA Cup Winners' Cup]], meaning a return to European football for the club following an absence of 27 years.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=147}}</ref>

===21st century===

====UEFA Cup====

In the [[2001–02 UEFA Cup]], Kilmarnock travelled to [[Lurgan]] in Northern Ireland to play [[Glenavon F.C.|Glenavon]],<ref name="ReferenceG">{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=156}}</ref> winning 1–0 following a goal by [[Chris Innes]].<ref name="ReferenceG"/> In the return leg at Rugby Park, Kilmarnock won 1–0 following a goal from [[Ally Mitchell]].<ref name="ReferenceG"/> In their next match, Kilmarnock faced Norwegian club [[Viking FK]], securing a 1–1 draw at Rugby Park before suffering a 0–2 loss away from home and exiting the UEFA Cup.<ref name="ReferenceG"/> Kilmarnock won the [[Scottish Youth Cup]] in 2004, following a 1–0 victory over Rangers which was held at Rugby Park due to [[Hampden Park]] being unavailable to host the final.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cairns, Livingston |first1=Richard, John |title=Kilmarnock Football Club: 150 Years In the Making |date=2019 |publisher=Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. |page=162}}</ref>

====2007 and 2012 Scottish League Cup finals====
{{Further|2007 Scottish League Cup final|2012 Scottish League Cup final}}
[[File:2012SLCF.jpg|thumb|right|Scene from the [[2012 Scottish League Cup final]] in which Kilmarnock beat [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]] 1–0]]
Kilmarnock reached the [[2007 Scottish League Cup final]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/scot_cups/6309881.stm|title=Football – Scottish Cups – Kilmarnock 3–0 Falkirk|publisher=BBC|date=30 January 2007|access-date=30 January 2007|archive-date=16 January 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140116200736/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/scot_cups/6309881.stm|url-status=live}}</ref> but suffered a 5–1 defeat in the final by [[Hibernian F.C.|Hibernian]]. After selling [[Steven Naismith]] to [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] for a club-record fee in August 2007, ''Killie'' struggled in the [[2007–08 Scottish Premier League]], finishing in 11th place with 40 points. In January 2010, Kilmarnock were second bottom of the [[2009–10 Scottish Premier League]], with last placed [[Falkirk F.C.|Falkirk]] just two points behind. On 11 January 2010, Jim Jefferies left the club by "mutual consent" and [[Jimmy Calderwood]] was appointed manager. Kilmarnock then achieved a first win in nine years against [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]]. Continued poor form, however, meant a final day showdown at Rugby Park with Falkirk for SPL survival. Kilmarnock began the game with a two-point advantage over their rivals and a goalless draw on the day was good enough to secure top-flight football for another year. They ended the season with just 33 points, their worst points finish in the SPL.

After Calderwood left at the end of the season, [[Mixu Paatelainen]] was appointed manager for the next two years with an option for a third.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/teams/k/kilmarnock/8754914.stm|title=Football – Mixu Paatelainen is named as the new Kilmarnock manager|publisher=BBC|date=23 June 2010|access-date=11 December 2010|archive-date=22 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180622061921/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/teams/k/kilmarnock/8754914.stm|url-status=live}}</ref> Despite being the favourites for relegation that season, Kilmarnock finished the season in fifth position. Paatelainen left the club to become manager of [[Finland national football team|Finland]] and his assistant [[Kenny Shiels]] was appointed manager. Kilmarnock progressed to the [[2012 Scottish League Cup final]] with wins against [[Queen of the South F.C.|Queen of the South]], [[East Fife F.C.|East Fife]] and [[Ayr United F.C.|Ayr United]] in an [[Ayrshire derby]] at Hampden. Kilmarnock won the League Cup for the first time, as they defeated Celtic 1–0 in the final; [[Dieter Van Tornhout]] scored the only goal six minutes from time, with goalkeeper [[Cammy Bell]] named Man of the Match.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/soccer/match/_/gameId/337473|title=Celtic vs. Kilmarnock – Football Match Summary|date=18 March 2012|work=ESPN.com|access-date=2 November 2021|archive-date=2 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211102222801/https://www.espn.com/soccer/match/_/gameId/337473|url-status=live}}</ref> In June 2013, after three years at Kilmarnock, manager [[Kenny Shiels]] was sacked by chairman Michael Johnston after a "mutual agreement" between the two.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/22855329|title=Kilmarnock part company with manager Kenny Shiels|publisher=BBC Sport|date=11 June 2013|access-date=12 February 2018|archive-date=25 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131225034842/http://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/0/football/22855329|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.heraldscotland.com/sport/opinion/spiers-on-sport-the-unjust-sacking-of-kenny-shiels.1371051762|title=Spiers on Sport: the unjust sacking of Kenny Shiels|work=The Herald|date=12 June 2013|location=Glasgow|access-date=13 June 2013|archive-date=15 June 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130615043751/http://www.heraldscotland.com/sport/opinion/spiers-on-sport-the-unjust-sacking-of-kenny-shiels.1371051762|url-status=live}}</ref>

====Manager changes====

[[Allan Johnston]] signed a two-year contract and was appointed manager on 24 June 2013, with [[Sandy Clark]] as the assistant manager.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.qosfc.com/new_newsview.aspx?newsid=1846|title=Allan Johnston Joins Kilmarnock|publisher=qosfc.com|access-date=24 June 2013|archive-date=17 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150417110759/http://www.qosfc.com/new_newsview.aspx?newsid=1846|url-status=dead}}</ref> Clark left his role in the summer of 2014 with the club looking to go in a new direction, and ex-Killie player and former Hearts manager [[Gary Locke (Scottish footballer)|Gary Locke]] was appointed as his assistant. Johnston was sacked in February 2015 after informing the press of his intention to leave in the summer, before discussing this with the board. Locke was placed in interim charge, before signing a three-year deal in April 2015.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/32157590|title=Kilmarnock: Gary Locke confirmed as permanent manager|date=3 April 2015|publisher=BBC Sport|access-date=12 February 2018|archive-date=19 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181219082609/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/32157590|url-status=live}}</ref> Kilmarnock went on to lose seven of their final eight games of the season, but were spared the play-off spot after a 4–1 win over [[Partick Thistle F.C.|Partick Thistle]].

The 2015–16 season would prove difficult for the team. Locke was removed from his position as manager in February 2016, with [[Lee Clark (footballer)|Lee Clark]] being appointed as his replacement.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/35582156|title=Lee Clark: Who is the new Kilmarnock manager?|last=Sutherland|first=Jonathan|date=15 February 2016|publisher=[[BBC Sport]]|access-date=25 October 2016|archive-date=25 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170225180549/http://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/35582156|url-status=live}}</ref> Despite a small uplift in form, the team finished in 11th place and faced a relegation play-off against Championship side Falkirk in order to stay in the top flight. Despite losing 0–1 in the first leg, ''Killie'' fought back and comfortably won the second leg 4–0 (4–1 on aggregate), securing the club's status in the Scottish Premiership for another season. Clark would leave Kilmarnock for a return to England with [[Bury F.C.|Bury]] in February 2017, exactly a year after his arrival.<ref name="Clark to Bury">{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/38984096 |title=Lee Clark: Kilmarnock boss to quit to join Bury |publisher=BBC Sport |date=15 February 2017 |access-date=15 February 2017 |archive-date=15 February 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170215191427/http://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/38984096 |url-status=live }}</ref> Former Rangers player [[Lee McCulloch]], assistant to both Locke and Clark, was placed in temporary charge until the end of the season, achieving an eighth-place finish. The following season saw another poor start, with an early defeat to rivals [[Ayr United F.C.|Ayr United]] in the league cup group stages, followed by a disappointing start to the league campaign. McCulloch was sacked in September 2017 with the club rooted to the bottom of the table.

====The Clarke era====
{{Further|2019–20 UEFA Europa League|Kilmarnock F.C. in European football}}
[[File:Steve Clarke 2019.jpg|thumb|right|140px|[[Steve Clarke]], appointed manager in 2017, led the club to 3rd place in the [[2018–19 Scottish Premiership]] and secured a place in the [[2019–20 UEFA Europa League]]]]
In an unexpected move, Kilmarnock appointed former [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]] and [[West Bromwich Albion F.C.|West Bromwich Albion]] coach [[Steve Clarke]]. It was Clarke's first involvement with the Scottish game in 30 years and his appointment preempted a dramatic upturn in form, with the club ultimately finishing in fifth place, earning him the SFWA Manager of the Year award in the process.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.scottishfwa.com/news/2018/5/13/clarke-is-manager-of-the-year|title=Clarke is manager of the year|date=13 May 2018|publisher=[[Scottish Football Writers' Association|SFWA]]|access-date=5 May 2020|archive-date=14 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190514215608/https://www.scottishfwa.com/news/2018/5/13/clarke-is-manager-of-the-year|url-status=live}}</ref> The 2018–19 season saw Kilmarnock celebrate their 150th anniversary, and the team continued their strong form in the league, both home and away, culminating in a final day fixture against [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] at Rugby Park. Kilmarnock won the match 2–1 and the result secured a third-place finish in the league, which guaranteed European football for the first time since 2001. The season's results also set a new record points total for the club and their highest placed finish in the league since 1966. The following day, Clarke was signed by the [[Scottish Football Association]] to become the head coach of the [[Scotland national football team|Scotland national team]].

Following the departure of Steve Clarke, Kilmarnock had three managers whose spell in charge was brief, beginning with former [[Juventus FC|Juventus]] and Chelsea assistant coach [[Angelo Alessio]]. In Alessio's second match in charge, Kilmarnock lost in Europa League qualification to [[Cymru Premier|Welsh Premier League]] club [[Connah's Quay Nomads F.C.|Connah's Quay Nomads]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/48970490|title=Kilmarnock 0−2 Connah's Quay Nomads: Scots stunned by Welsh|date=18 July 2019|publisher=BBC|access-date=20 April 2021|archive-date=19 July 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190719020955/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/48970490|url-status=live}}</ref> Alessio was sacked in December 2019, with the team sitting in fifth place.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/50822801 |title=Angelo Alessio: Italian sacked as Kilmarnock manager |publisher=BBC Sport |date=17 December 2019 |access-date=17 December 2019 |archive-date=17 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191217132320/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/50822801 |url-status=live }}</ref> Following his departure, [[Alex Dyer (footballer, born 1965)|Alex Dyer]], assistant coach to both Alessio and Clarke, was appointed on an initial caretaker basis until the end of the season, before all football was abruptly ended due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. Dyer's services were retained by the club and he signed a new contract extension in June 2020.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/53049501 |title=Alex Dyer: Kilmarnock boss 'chuffed' to continue as right-back Aaron McGowan signs |publisher=BBC Sport |date=15 June 2020 |access-date=20 April 2021 |archive-date=20 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210420153523/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/53049501 |url-status=live }}</ref> However, following a poor start to the new season, he left the club by mutual consent in January 2021.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/55873331 |title=Alex Dyer: Kilmarnock boss leaves post 'by mutual consent' after St Johnstone collapse |publisher=BBC Sport |date=30 January 2021 |access-date=20 April 2021 |archive-date=30 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210130185146/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/55873331 |url-status=live }}</ref> In February 2021, former [[St Johnstone F.C.|St Johnstone]] manager [[Tommy Wright (footballer, born 1963)|Tommy Wright]] was appointed as the club's third manager in two years.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/55963647 |title=Tommy Wright: Kilmarnock appoint Northern Irishman as Alex Dyer's successor |publisher=BBC Sport |date=8 February 2021 |access-date=20 April 2021 |archive-date=7 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210207215643/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/55963647 |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 24 May 2021, following a play−off defeat to [[Dundee F.C.|Dundee]], Kilmarnock were relegated to the [[Scottish Championship]], bringing an end to their 28-year stay in the top flight.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/57139366 |title=Kilmarnock 1−2 Dundee (2−4): Dundee relegate Kilmarnock, earn promotion |publisher=BBC Sport |date=24 May 2021 |access-date=29 May 2021 |archive-date=23 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210523212532/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/57139366 |url-status=live }}</ref> Their 11th-place finish and play-off defeat in [[2020–21 Kilmarnock F.C. season|2020–21]] meant it was the club's first season in the Championship, and their first in the second tier of Scottish football since [[1992–93 Scottish First Division|1992–93]]. ==Ayrshire Derby==
{{main|Ayrshire derby}} 
[[File:AyrshireDerby.JPG|thumb|left|Kilmarnock and [[Ayr United F.C.|Ayr United]] line up for an Ayrshire derby match at [[Hampden Park]], 2012]]

Kilmarnock's biggest rivalry is with their South Ayrshire neighbours, [[Ayr United F.C.|Ayr United]], and together they contest the [[Ayrshire derby]]. Between national competitions such as the [[Scottish Football League]], [[Scottish Cup]], [[Scottish League Cup]] and the [[Scottish Challenge Cup]], Kilmarnock have beaten Ayr United a total of 59 times, whilst beating Ayr United 43 times in defunct competitions such as the [[Ayrshire Cup]], Ayrshire League, Ayr Charity Cup, Kilmarnock Charity Cup and the West Sound Trophy.<ref>{{cite web |title=Kilmarnock F.C. Results |url=https://www.fitbastats.com/kilmarnock/team_results_list.php?opposition=22&from=133&to=148&competition=35&venue=0&update=Update |publisher=Fitbastats |access-date=14 October 2023 |archive-date=24 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231024134509/https://www.fitbastats.com/kilmarnock/team_results_list.php?opposition=22&from=133&to=148&competition=35&venue=0&update=Update |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 28 January 2012, Ayr United and Kilmarnock met at [[Hampden Park]] for the League Cup semi-final. Kilmarnock won 1–0 thanks to a 109th-minute goal from [[Dean Shiels]].<ref name=lc2012>{{cite news|url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/16664409|title= Ayr United 0–1 Kilmarnock|publisher= BBC Sport|date= 28 January 2011|access-date= 1 December 2017|archive-date= 4 February 2013|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130204044637/http://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/0/football/16664409|url-status= live}}</ref> This was the first time that the Ayrshire derby had taken place in the semi-finals of a major competition<ref>{{cite web|title=Ayrshire's bitter derby reaches Hampden|url=http://www.wsc.co.uk/wsc-daily/1023-January-2012/8239-ayrshires-bitter-derby-reaches-hampden|access-date=23 January 2018|publisher=[[When Saturday Comes]]|date=26 January 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180124070852/http://www.wsc.co.uk/wsc-daily/1023-January-2012/8239-ayrshires-bitter-derby-reaches-hampden|archive-date=24 January 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> and it was also the first derby to be played at a neutral venue. The game also achieved the highest recorded post-[[World War II]] crowd of any Ayrshire derby with 25,057 people travelling to Hampden (Kilmarnock versus Ayr United on 19 March 1938 had a crowd of 27,442).

The Ayrshire Derby fixture was revived in season 2021–22, as both clubs were in the same division following Kilmarnock's relegation to the [[Scottish Championship]].

==Club operations==
===Ownership and finances===
Since June 1906, Kilmarnock F.C. has been owned by the private limited company, The Kilmarnock Football Club Ltd. Since 2014, the majority shareholder of the club is Ayrshire businessman Billy Bowie, who oversees all operations of the club.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/SC006219/officers|title=The Kilmarnock Football Club Limited|date=15 February 2016|website=gov.uk|access-date=11 February 2021|archive-date=21 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210921140613/https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/SC006219/officers|url-status=live}}</ref> Kilmarnock became debt-free under Bowie's control in 2017 after several years of financial difficulty.

In May 2018 Kilmarnock made a landmark move by appointing Phyllis McLeish, commercial director of the QTS Group, to the club's board; in doing so she became the first female board member in over 20 years. Later that same month, the club appointed its second female board member in [[Cathy Jamieson]], former MP for the [[Kilmarnock and Loudoun (UK Parliament constituency)|Kilmarnock and Loudoun district]] and a life-long Killie fan. Her appointment came after being nominated by The Killie Trust Initiative, who raised over £100,000 to have a member of the trust on the board.

===Colours and badge===
[[File:Kilmarnock_FC_150th_Anniversary_Logo.svg|thumb|left|The 150th Anniversary Badge used from 2018 to 2020]]

The earliest known Kilmarnock kit from 1879 consisted of an all-blue jersey with white trousers. The shirt bore a crest which was described as "a hand, index and second fingers upright, thumb outstretched, other fingers enclosed over a palm" (an adoption of the historic [[Clan Boyd]] chief's heraldic crest). The hand rested on a bar over a ball marked KFC. Between 1887 and 1890 Kilmarnock wore black and white striped tops. Thereafter, the club has predominantly played in blue and white striped or hooped shirts with either blue or white shorts. The club have also occasionally played in plain blue and plain white tops; this was suggested by Ross Quigley who, at the time, was one of the first directors of the club, although the kit was later changed to the hooped style in 1920. The club's away colours have varied greatly over time. Yellow is generally regarded as the club's main third colour; but white, red and purple away kits have also appeared in recent years.

Between 2008 and 2014, the club manufactured their kits under their own sportswear brand, 1869. Following this, Italian company Erreá was the manufacturer. Kilmarnock kits were manufactured by American company [[Nike, Inc.|Nike]] between 2016 and 2020. The current kit manufacturer is Danish company [[Hummel International|Hummel]]; it can only be bought from the store at [[Rugby Park]].

The club badge is a modernised version of previous club badges. It features a ball bearing a hand in a blessing position, flanked by two red squirrels. The club's Latin motto, ''confidemus'' (we trust), is written above the badge (similar to the [[Clan Boyd]] heraldic motto, ''confido'' (I trust)). The club adopted the badge in 1992 after [[Lord Lyon King of Arms|The Lord Lyon]] decreed that the previous badge, based heavily upon the town crest, was in breach of ancient Scottish [[heraldry|heraldic]] rules.

In October 2018 the club unveiled a special badge for the club's 150th anniversary.

===Club mascot===
The club's mascot is a squirrel named 'Captain Conker', named after the squirrels which feature on the club's crest and the coat of arms of the [[Clan Boyd]] of Kilmarnock. In the past, the 'Killie Pie' mascot was also a regular at Rugby Park on matchdays. Previously, the mascot was Nutz the squirrel, played by long-time Kilmarnock fan Ian Downie who died in 2020. Downie had played the club's mascot for 19 years prior to his death.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Highet |first1=Lochlin |title=Heartfelt tributes pour in for man behind Kilmarnock's Nutz mascot of 19 years |url=https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/ayrshire/heartfelt-tributes-pour-man-behind-22868211 |website=www.dailyrecord.co.uk |publisher=Daily Record |access-date=1 March 2024 |language=en |date=19 October 2020}}</ref>

===Stadium===
{{Further|Rugby Park}}
[[File:Rugby Park, Kilmarnock.jpg|thumb|left|240px|[[Rugby Park]] stadium, situated on Rugby Road, home of Kilmarnock FC]]
Kilmarnock first played football matches at the present [[Rugby Park]] site in 1899. Despite this, the venue is actually Kilmarnock's fourth home ground. The Grange, Holm Quarry and Ward's Park all hosted matches before the club moved to Rugby Park in 1877. This was not the present stadium, but one situated close by near South Hamilton Street. This ground was shared by cricket and rugby teams – sports which Kilmarnock had played previously – and the connection with rugby gave the ground its name. This name was taken with the club when they moved to their present stadium.

During the 1994–95 season the stadium capacity was significantly reduced as three new stands were constructed; the Moffat Stand, the Chadwick Stand and the East Stand. Their completion brought the capacity of the stadium to {{SPFL-stadiums|kilmarnock}}.<ref name="capacity">{{cite web |url=http://spfl.co.uk/clubs/kilmarnock/ |title=Kilmarnock Football Club |publisher=Scottish Professional Football League |access-date=30 September 2013 |archive-date=3 May 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170503043137/http://spfl.co.uk/clubs/kilmarnock/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The stadium opened on 6 August 1995, in a friendly match against English champions [[Blackburn Rovers F.C.|Blackburn Rovers]]. [[Mike Newell (footballer)|Mike Newell]] hit a hat-trick as the home team lost 5–0.

A [[FIFA]] 2 star [[FieldTurf]] [[Artificial turf|artificial pitch]] was installed at Rugby Park for the start of the [[2014–15 Kilmarnock F.C. season|2014–15]] season. The pitch was capable of hosting [[rugby football|rugby]] matches as well as football. A new artificial hybrid surface was installed during the 2019 close season. In February 2019 Kilmarnock received approval to install a new safe-standing section in areas of the East and Moffat stands. The installation process was completed in early December of that year.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/48612693 |title=Kilmarnock U16s safe-standing section is British first |publisher=BBC Sport |date=12 June 2019 |access-date=4 March 2020 |archive-date=7 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200807164535/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/48612693 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In December 2022 Kilmarnock announced that consultation had begun on the plans to develop 'Bowie Park Training Facility'<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fitzsimmons |first=Andrew |date=2022-12-13 |title=Consultation begins on plans to develop 'Bowie Park Training Facility' |url=https://kilmarnockfc.co.uk/news/consultation-begins-on-plans-to-develop-bowie-park-training-facility/ |access-date=2023-03-15 |website=Kilmarnock FC |language=en |archive-date=15 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230315125821/https://kilmarnockfc.co.uk/news/consultation-begins-on-plans-to-develop-bowie-park-training-facility/ |url-status=live }}</ref> with a view to creating a dedicated club training ground where Kilmarnock's men's, women's and academy teams develop within the same purpose-built environment. Funded by [[Billy Bowie]], the development features two five-a-side and two full-size pitches – one with an accompanying 500-seat stand – alongside a two-floor training facility building which hosts a gym, changing rooms, canteen / seminar room, offices and a players' lounge.

===Club anthem===
The song "[[Paper Roses]]", originally a hit by American singer and activist [[Anita Bryant]], was adopted by Kilmarnock fans as their own club anthem. American singer and actress [[Marie Osmond]], who is famous for recording this song, surprised the fans in February 2013 and performed at Rugby Park along with a meet and greet session, signing autographs for the players and fans.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kilmarnockfc.co.uk/Article?id=506|title=Marie Osmond visits Kilmarnock Football Club.|access-date=12 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161022082618/http://www.kilmarnockfc.co.uk/Article?id=506|archive-date=22 October 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>
